NYG are soft against the run (142 yds/game allowed), and DAL feed Javonte Williams a heavy 62% carry share — a rushing-yards spot.

The NYG welcome the DAL as underdogs of 1.5, with the total set at 48.5 — a market that implies a DAL 25–24 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 26% of its snaps with DAL in front, 39% within one score, and 34% with DAL chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

This is a coin-flip script. With only 1.5 points separating them, neither team projects to spend much time in a blowout state — most of the game lives in the 'close' bucket, where play-calling stays balanced and usage tracks each player's established role rather than being distorted by score. In tight games the stars on both sides see their normal, dependable workloads, and there is less garbage-time leakage to backups.

The Key Matchups

Jaxson Dart has a passing-yards tailwind — DAL allow 252 pass yds/game (vs ~230).

Sneaky value on Darius Slayton (WR2) — DAL leak 43 yds/game to the WR2 role, above the ~36 norm.

Tyrone Tracy Jr. eats as a receiver too — DAL give up 29 rec yds/game to backs, and NYG target the RB on 18% of throws.

Touchdown Board

Malik Nabers carries TD equity — DAL surrender 0.59 WR1 receiving scores a game.

In the red zone DAL throw it (58% pass inside the 20) — CeeDee Lamb's TD equity over a goal-line back.

Game Script, Pace & Environment

Shootout profile — a 48 total between two non-run-first offenses points to volume passing on both sides; lean into the overs for the pass-catchers.

DAL — a balanced offense

DAL are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (44% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

Javonte Williams (13 carries, 53 yards) projects to his baseline workload — no strong script push either way in a close game.

CeeDee Lamb projects for 6 targets and 58 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, Jake Ferguson (TE, 4 targets, 23 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

NYG — a balanced offense

NYG are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (42% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

Tyrone Tracy Jr. (12 carries, 53 yards) projects to his baseline workload — no strong script push either way in a close game.

Malik Nabers projects for 8 targets and 60 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

Underneath, Theo Johnson (TE, 5 targets, 41 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 2-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.
